name: KV-cache offload to a CPU/DRAM tier: bytes over PCIe, why it is bandwidth-bound, and when it beats recompute
arithmetic_intensity: AI = 0 in the strict sense - offload is a DMA copy with no arithmetic - so cost = KV bytes / PCIe bandwidth, and the useful question is never 'how fast is the copy' but 'is the copy cheaper than the recompute it replaces'. That comparison is a flop-versus-byte trade between two different roofs: recomputing a KV block costs ~2 x active_params x block_tokens FLOPs on the compute roof, while loading it costs C_block bytes over the PCIe roof. vLLM's docs make offload DMA-based and asynchronous ('Transfers between GPU and CPU use DMA (cudaMemcpyAsync) and run asynchronously alongside model computation, so offloading adds minimal CPU- and GPU-core overhead'), which is what makes the offload direction nearly free and the load direction the one that costs TTFT. The vendor's own measured claim is a ratio, not a bandwidth: loading from the CPU tier 'reduces TTFT by X2-X22' depending on prompt size (H100, 500GB DRAM, GPU prefix caching disabled so CPU hits are isolated).
scales_with: kv_bytes_resident (linear in context_length x live sequences - offload is a capacity mechanism, so the volume is whatever does not fit in HBM)
pcie_generation_and_width (Gen4 x16 vs Gen5 x16 is roughly a 2x difference and it is the dominant term in the load path)
block_size / blocks_per_chunk (larger chunks amortise per-transfer overhead into larger, more efficient host I/Os)
host_dram_capacity (how much can be kept resident rather than staged)
gpu_preemption_rate (the win case: preempted sequences would otherwise recompute)
tier_depth (anything below the CPU primary tier costs two hops, since only CPU has direct GPU access)
workarounds: Async DMA offload with prefetch so a cold cache never stalls the step (vLLM OffloadingConnector; CUDA/ROCm/XPU only)
Offload before preemption so a preempted sequence resumes instead of recomputing - the win case the vLLM blog leads with
Use the CPU tier as the mandatory staging tier for deeper tiers, and accept the two-hop cost rather than assuming a direct SSD path (TieringOffloadingSpec)
Cap per-request offload/load with max_offload_tokens and max_load_tokens so one long request cannot evict the hot set for everyone
fp8 or int8 KV cache to halve the bytes that cross PCIe
Keep the hot prefix on GPU and use the DRAM tier only for the cold tail - the tier only helps once the hot set fits in HBM
notes: When it wins, per vLLM's own blog, is NOT primarily 'requests share a common prefix' - that is the prefix-cache argument, and the blog explicitly separates the two cases: 'KV cache offloading can be useful even for workloads where requests share no common prefix', because under high concurrency the GPU runs out of KV, the engine preempts a running request and discards its KV, and 'the cost for re-computing the KV values can be avoided by offloading the KV cache to a larger tier (such as CPU DRAM) before the request is pre-empted'. So the honest statement of the win condition is: long context (large C_block) plus low batch (idle compute to trade) plus preemption pressure. When it loses: when the hot working set fits in HBM anyway (the transfer is pure overhead), when the request is short (fixed transfer overhead dominates a small block), and when the working set is so large that the DRAM tier thrashes - note the deeper-tier structure means anything below CPU pays GPU->CPU->SSD, so a slow SSD is worse than no tier. Portability bound worth stating plainly: vLLM's OffloadingConnector 'currently supports CUDA, ROCm, and XPU only'. The failure mode that follows from offload is correctness, not speed: a KV tier that serves a block which does not match the current model, adapter, layout or kernel configuration produces wrong output with no error. See the LMCache packed-layout corruption gotcha and vLLM #58263 on the missing compatibility fields in the offload namespace.
